title: California grassland plots kept a shift to warm-niche species after the 2012-2015 drought; weather did not explain it, but it was not clearly above random-niche drift (13 series, 1983-2021)
abstract: Question: was the reported shift of California grassland plots to species from warmer and drier places (higher community temperature index, CTI; lower precipitation index, CPI) a short response to weather and the 2012-2015 drought, or a persistent change? Data: the public release of Zhu, Song et al. 2024 (12 observational sites plus Jasper Ridge experiment ambient plots; 192 site-years, 1983-2021), Daymet weather and nClimGrid temperature. A test plan was written before outcome models were fitted. Results: rain and temperature explained 3.6% of within-site CTI variation. At the four series with 2016-2019 surveys, CTI was +0.19 C above the pre-drought mean during the drought and +0.22 C after it (pooled return fraction -0.17), although a weather model expected a return. The CTI trend was +0.160 C per decade (location-bootstrap interval 0.088 to 0.372), +0.164 with weather terms and +0.126 before 2012. Pre-2012 site trends forecast 2012-2019 CTI better (RMSE 0.165 C) than the pre-2012 mean (0.290), recent persistence (0.246) or a weather model (0.316). However, random niche labels on the same abundance changes gave trends with SD 0.105 C per decade: one-sided p = 0.069 (0.128 inside guilds). The CPI decrease (-29.5 mm per decade) was more clearly niche-related (p = 0.029). A few grasses carried the CTI change (exotic Brachypodium distachyon and Bromus diandrus up, native Danthonia californica and Poa secunda down); without the top three contributors the trend was +0.046 (interval -0.148 to 0.174). Site CTI trends correlated weakly with local warming (r = 0.26). Conclusion: the shift was persistent and directional and did not reverse after the drought, which rejects the transient-weather explanation, but its CTI part is not clearly larger than random-niche drift and could also come from grass invasion and perennial loss. Limitations: only three locations with post-drought surveys, occurrence-based niches, no grazing or fire data.
